salt_presence.description: Indicates whether salt is present (true) or not (false) in the water.

message.content:
The color of the sea isn’t a single, fixed hue—it changes with depth, light, water composition, and what’s floating in it. In general:

| Depth | Typical Color | Why |
|-------|---------------|-----|
| **Shallow, clear water** | Turquoise / light blue | Light penetrates easily; scattering of shorter wavelengths (blue) dominates, while some green light is also reflected. |
| **Mid‑depth, clear water** | Deep blue | As depth increases, longer wavelengths (red, orange, yellow) are absorbed, leaving mostly blue light. |
| **Coastal waters with algae or phytoplankton** | Greenish‑blue | Chlorophyll absorbs red and blue light, reflecting green. |
| **Water with suspended sediments or organic matter** | Brownish or muddy | Particles scatter all wavelengths, giving a more muted, brownish tone. |
| **Very deep ocean** | Dark navy or almost black | Most visible light is absorbed; only a faint blue remains. |

So, the “color of the sea” depends on where you’re looking and what’s in the water. In a textbook sense, we often describe it as “blue,” but in reality it can range from turquoise to green to brown to almost black.
